newsitem.title: GUAM: Rescuers seek Guam survivors under floodlights.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers seek Guam survivors under floodlights.

text.p: Rescuers worked through the night under floodlights to try to find survivors amid the wreckage of a Korean Air Lines jumbo jet carrying 254 passengers that crashed on the Pacific island of Guam on Wednesday.
But officials said the effort was being hampered by the difficulty of reaching the site in rough terrain and by the inclement weather.
There were conflicting reports on the number of survivors in the crash.
Andrew Murphy, spokesman for the Guam Airport Authority told Reuters: "We believe there are 29 to 30 survivors and most have been taken to the Navy medical centre,"
But David Furlong, editor of the Pacific Navigator, a military newspaper, said 19 passengers had been taken to the Navy Hospital and 40 more survivors were being transported.
As dawn broke over the Pacific island territory, what appeared to be a wing and other fragments of wreckage were silhouetted against the trees on the hillside near Guam's Agana airport.
Rescuers used floodlights to illuminate the crash site located in rough terrain in a sparsely populated area called Nimitz, some seven miles (12 km) south of the airport.
Murphy said the flight recorder of the aircraft, which was en route to Guam from Seoul, had been found and was being sent to the airport for safekeeping.
Weather in the region was inclement, with typhoon Nina with top winds of 85 mph (145 kph) veering away from the northern Philippines towards Japan.
It was cloudy and raining heavily, and visibility was poor. Aviation sources there had been reports of flights being delayed because of the weather.
Murphy said it was also not clear whether first word of the crash had come from an emergency message from the aircraft or from eyewitnesses on the ground.
"At this time, everything is still speculation," he said.

A spokesman for Boeing Co said the jet involved was a Boeing 747-300 delivered to Korean Air Lines in December 1984. The jet had accumulated just under 50,000 hours of flight time in 8,433 flights or "cycles", he said.

FAA spokesman Eliot Brenner said the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board would investigate the crash with participation of the Federal Aviation Administration. He said the FAA had no firm number for the number on board.
An FAA spokeswoman later said the plane had just been cleared for landing at 2.35 a.m. on Wednesday (12.35 p.m. EDT on Tuesday, 1625 GMT on Tuesday) when radar contact was lost.

Guam, largest of the Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific, is an unincorporated territory of the United States with a population of about 144,000. A U.S. military base covers about one-third of the island.
